title: Nudging consumers towards healthier choices: a systematic review of positional influences on food choice
abstract: Nudging or 'choice architecture' refers to strategic changes in the environment that are anticipated to alter people's behaviour in a predictable way, without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives. Nudging strategies may be used to promote healthy eating behaviour. However, to date, the scientific evidence has not been systematically reviewed to enable practitioners and policymakers to implement, or argue for the implementation of, specific measures to support nudging strategies. This systematic review investigated the effect of positional changes of food placement on food choice. In total, seven scientific databases were searched using relevant keywords to identify interventions that manipulated food position (proximity or order) to generate a change in food selection, sales or consumption, among normal-weight or overweight individuals across any age group. From 2576 identified articles, fifteen articles comprising eighteen studies met our inclusion criteria. This review has identified that manipulation of food product order or proximity can influence food choice. Such approaches offer promise in terms of impacting on consumer behaviour. However, there is a need for high-quality studies that quantify the magnitude of positional effects on food choice in conjunction with measuring the impact on food intake, particularly in the longer term. Future studies should use outcome measures such as change in grams of food consumed or energy intake to quantify the impact on dietary intake and potential impacts on nutrition-related health. Research is also needed to evaluate potential compensatory behaviours secondary to such interventions.

claims.text: Out of eighteen included studies evaluating food position or order manipulation, sixteen found a positive influence on food choice.
The two studies that found no significant effect of positional changes on snack choice manipulated only minor order changes within arm's reach.
Only one of the eighteen included studies received a positive quality rating, with fourteen rated as neutral and three as negative.
Moving potato chips to a more distant location reduced potato chip selection but was accompanied by an increase in starch selection.
Distance from a serving bowl significantly predicted the number of crackers and carrot slices consumed by children.

limitations.text: A meta-analysis could not be conducted because study designs and reported outcome measures were too heterogeneous.
The review did not consider grey literature, raising the plausibility of positive publication bias.
Assortment structure and supermarket shopping literature were beyond the review's scope, which focused primarily on out-of-home meal service situations.
Included studies lacked long-term evaluations, making it unclear whether positional effects persist over time or decay.
Most included studies assessed selection frequencies rather than objectively quantifying intake in grams or energy content.
Included studies rarely evaluated compensatory consumption behaviors occurring after positional nudges.

future_work.text: Conduct high-quality studies measuring food intake using standardized quantitative indicators like grams consumed or energy intake (kJ/kcal) over longer time horizons.
Investigate potential compensatory eating behaviors that may occur secondary to positional nudge interventions.
Examine covariates such as dietary preferences, restrained/disinhibited eating styles, health consciousness, and habit strength via customer loyalty card schemes.
Clearly distinguish and standardize keywords and reporting terminology between food order nudges (driven by salience) and food distance/proximity nudges (driven by effort).

methodologies.name: Systematic literature review following PICOS framework
methodologies.description: Searched seven electronic databases up to February 2015 to evaluate experimental and observational studies assessing microenvironmental food positioning (proximity or order) on food choice without confounding multi-variable manipulations.
conditions: Manipulated food position (proximity or order) within microenvironments
Targeted healthy, normal-weight or overweight/obese participants across any age group
Excluded studies manipulating multiple simultaneous variables (e.g. adding/removing food items or changing portion sizes)
